synopsis: The strategy requires virtual testing to improve the new collision-mitigation system to meet or beat the current system and to tune thresholds and calibration before field testing; previous physical testing and tuning took three to four years per machine model [f27, f29, f8252]. On-road precedents demonstrate threshold evaluation, including a 2019 sweep of time-to-collision triggers and latencies, but no published quantitative off-road comparison with field results was found, leaving transferability unknown and constituting the programme’s main technical risk [f6346, f6558, f155]. Tuning should pursue multiple objectives under hard safety constraints rather than start with one weighted cost, and should prefer broad stable operating regions over fragile optima; detector operating-point tuning alone misses closed-loop timing and braking [f6959, f6963, f6989, f7304]. Settings include confidence thresholds, speed-dependent zones, confirmation filters and timing constants, while intervention staging should use remaining stopping margin and uncertainty rather than range alone [f6957, f6280]. Virtual tuning can explore trigger structure, grade and payload dependence and initial zone sizes, but production brake characteristics, real-site friction, adverse-condition sensor behaviour and nuisance rates require measurements and shadow-mode logs; a 2026 on-road round robin also found simulator disagreements of 0.033 seconds and 0.314 metres [f14054, f14055, f14048]. The proposed sequence is to freeze the decision architecture and sweep scenarios before hardware arrives, reserve the first six weeks after delivery for physical anchoring, then rerun calibrated sweeps and measure nuisance rates in shadow mode before enabling braking; requirements definition and field tuning may remain the real bottleneck [f14056, f14057, f14058, f10859].
